How to make the Best Homemade Bacon (with Szechuan Peppercorns)

Using a food scale, weigh the pork belly. Use this weight to calculate the remaining ingredient amounts. For example, if you have 1000 g of pork belly, 2% salt = 20 g. Once you’ve weighed out the salt, celery powder, brown sugar, peppercorns, and garlic cloves, add them to a bowl and mix them all together.

Cover the pig belly with the cure mixture until completely covered. Vacuum seal the belly in a bag and let cure for around 7 days in the fridge (36-40°F/2-5°C) until the meat has firmed up and deepened in color. If you don’t have a vacuum sealer, you can cure the belly in freezer bags or a covered container. Just make sure the pork belly is well covered by the cure and rotate as needed to keep it covered by the cure. It’s normal for the cure to draw out moisture and turn it into a syrupy consistency. For very large pork belly sections (more than 5 kg/10 lbs), the curing time should be longer and might take up to two weeks.

After curing, it is time to smoke. Use an electric smoker, or a charcoal grill set up on indirect heat. Warm smoke the bacon somewhere between 73-104°F/22-40°C for at least 12 but up to 24 hours. This “warm” smoking temperature imparts a smoky flavor and dehydrates the meat but does not cook the bacon. After smoking, remove the skin and let it cool before slicing.
Slice the bacon as desired and cook when needed. Freeze & store extra slices.
My favorite recipe from my Grandma: Belish | Slovak Comfort Food

Warm the milk in the microwave until luke-warm (100°F/38°C). Add the instant yeast and stir together. Set aside and let activate for 5-10 minutes. Mix the flour, salt, and sugar in a large bowl. Meanwhile, remove the skin from the potatoes and cube them up.

Pour the yeast and milk into the dry ingredients. Add in the melted butter and beaten eggs. Mix the dough together with your hands until a shaggy dough forms. It will be very sticky. Put saran wrap over the bowl and let rest for 20-30 minutes.

While the dough is resting, add the potatoes to a pot and cover with water. Bring them to a boil and continue to cook until they can easily be mashed with a fork. Strain the potatoes off and add them back to the pot. Mash the potatoes and incorporate the cheese Taste them. Add salt as needed. Let cool.

With dough rested, add flour to the work surface. Turn the dough onto the floured counter and knead by hand for at least 10 minutes. Set a timer if needed. After kneading, the dough ball should be completely smooth. Add the dough to a bowl and cover with plastic wrap. Let the dough rise until doubled, around 45-60 minutes.

When the dough doubles, turn it out and cut into two pieces. Flatten the dough by hand and thin out the edges. Add half of the potato filling and fold the sides up around the dough like a large dumpling. Do the same with the other piece of dough. Let rest for 20 minutes. Preheat the oven to 400°F/ 204°C. Using your hands, flatten the potato filled dough until about 1 inch thick. Move each of the belish to a buttered baking sheeting. Using a rolling pin, flatten the belish until it is about 1/2 inch thick.

Add the belish to the oven and bake for 10 minutes. Take it out and flip the belish. Rub butter on the top layer. Add back to the oven and bake for 10 more minutes. Flip and rub more butter on the top. Add a sprinkle of flakey salt. Cut into squares with a pizza cutter and enjoy.
How to make the SIMPLEST ITALIAN PASTA SAUCE at home

Crush the whole peeled tomatoes with a food mill, food processor, or blender until smooth. If you want a more rustic sauce, leave the tomatoes whole or chunky, and let them break down naturally during the cooking. Peel and cut the onion in half, but leave the root end attached so the onion doesn't fall apart during cooking.

Add the tomatoes, butter, peeled onion halves, and a small pinch of salt to a large skillet over medium-low heat. A wider skillet reduces sauce more effectively than a deep pot: the wider surface area evaporates moisture more easily. Stirring occasionally, let the sauce simmer until it is reduced and thickened, about 30 minutes.
Turn off the heat and fish out the onion halves (you can eat or discard these). Taste the sauce and add salt as needed. Use immediately, or store the sauce in the fridge for about a week.
The Fish Guide - Everything you need to know
300g starchy (floury) potatoes (Sebago, Coliban, Russet Burbank, King Edward)
340g tuna in spring water, well drained
sea salt and freshly ground black pepper, to season
wilted spinach and tartare sauce, to serve
Peel and chop the potatoes. Place in a large saucepan of cold salted water and place over high heat. Bring to a boil and cook for around 15 minutes, until tender.
Drain the potatoes well in a colander, then steam over the hot saucepan (off the heat) for a couple of minutes.
Transfer to a bowl and mash until smooth.
Chop the leek and wash in a colander to remove any dirt. Melt the butter in a frying pan over medium heat.
Add the leek and season with some salt. Sweat the leeks gently for 6 minutes, until soft. Set aside to cool slightly.
Finely chop the chives and parsley leaves. Add to the mashed potato along with the leeks, tuna, the zest and juice of the lemons and season with salt and pepper. Mix together until well combined.
Divide the mixture into 4 equal portions and shape into round discs. Place on a tray and freeze for 20 minutes maximum, or 2 hours in the fridge to firm up.
Place the beaten egg, flour and breadcrumbs in separate shallow bowls or small trays. Season the flour with some salt.
Dip the tuna patties in the flour, shaking off any excess, then coat in the egg, then the breadcrumbs. Place on a tray.
Heat enough oil in a large frying pan to shallow fry over medium heat. Add the patties and cook for 4-5 minutes on each side, until golden brown and crispy.
Remove from the pan and drain on some paper towel. Serve the fish cakes with some wilted spinach and tartare sauce on the side.
Recreating The Takeaway Pizza Of My Childhood
20ml olive oil, plus extra for greasing
Fresh diced pineapple, leg ham, grated mozzarella
Sliced Pepperino, BBQ sauce, bacon, sausage, seasoned beef mince
Combine the water, yeast and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with a dough hook. Mix on low speed to combine (about 1-2 minutes).
Add the flour and mix on medium-low speed for 5 minutes. Pour in the olive oil and salt and mix for a further 5 minutes, until smooth and elastic.
Transfer to your bench and bring it together with your hands until you have a lovely smooth surface and a nice tight ball (see cook support below if you need further instructions).
Transfer to a lightly oiled bowl, cover and set aside until doubled in size, 1-2 hours (depending on your room temperature).
Uncover the dough and knock back, then turn out onto a lightly floured work surface.
Divide the dough into 3 equal pieces (for 10in pieces) and roll each into a tight ball (or 2 pieces for larger 12in pizzas, see notes below).
Place on a lightly oiled tray with space in between for spreading. Lightly oil the tops of the dough and cover with some cling wrap.
Set aside to proof again, until doubled in size, about 30 mins to 1 hour.
Combine the canned tomatoes, tomato paste, oregano, basil, garlic powder, salt, sugar and pepper in a large saucepan. Place over a medium heat and bring to a simmer, mixing well.
Reduce the heat to medium-low, cover and simmer the sauce for 20 mins.
Remove from the heat and puree the sauce with a stick blender, until smooth. Set aside to cool completely.
Preheat the oven to 230°C (445°F) fan forced, if you have a pizza stone you can place this in the oven also.
Lightly dust 3 pizza trays with some semolina. (if you don't have pizza trays, baking trays will work)
Stretch the dough balls out on a lightly floured surface to a 10in (25cm) circle, creating a thick rim around the edge (about 20mm). Place on the prepared pizza tray.
Spread the base with some of the pizza sauce, leaving a 15mm border for the crust. Sprinkle over the cheese, then top with the diced tomato (or add your chosen toppings).
Bake for 10-12 minutes, until golden and base is cooked.
Slide the pizzas onto a large chopping board and slice into 8 pieces and serve.
My Favourite Vietnamese Beef Noodle Soup
4 sticks lemongrass, cut into 5 cm (2-inch) pieces
500g packet Bún bò Huế noodles (round rice noodles)
2 tbsp ground chilli (use less if you prefer it milder)
Add the beef ribs, beef bones, pork knuckle and trotters to a large stock pot and cover with cold water. Bring to a simmer and cook for 20 minutes, skimming off any scum that rises to the surface.
Drain and discard the water from the bones. Rinse the bones thoroughly, clean the pot, and add the bones back to the pot and put aside.
While the bones are simmering, heat the peanut oil in a medium saucepan over medium-low heat.

Add the annatto seeds, stirring frequently for 5 minutes. Add the ground chilli and stir to combine. Turn off the heat and leave to steep for 5-10 minutes, until the oil turns a deep red. Pass the oil through a sieve, discarding the seeds, then return the oil to the pan.
Peel and finely dice the garlic, finely dice the shallots and finely dice the lemongrass.
Place the annatto oil over medium heat. Add the lemongrass and sauté for 5-6 minutes, then add the shallots and continue cooking for a further 2 minutes.
Lastly, add the garlic and continue cooking for 4-5 minutes, until very fragrant.

Cut the lemongrass into 5cm (2in) pieces and add to the pot with the bones. Thickly slice the ginger and peel the onion and shallots. Add to the pot along with the fish sauce, fermented shrimp paste, rock sugar, salt, chicken bouillon and cover with fresh water about 10-12cms (5in) above the bones.
Add the sauteed aromats with the annatto oil.
Turn the heat to high until the broth starts to simmer, then turn to low and slowly simmer the broth for 6 hours.
After 3 hours, remove the pork knuckle and beef ribs from the pot and set aside. These will be sliced to serve later. (If you prefer your meat with a bit more chew, remove it after 1.5 hours instead)
Bring a large saucepan of salted water to a simmer over medium heat. Slice the ginger, smash the garlic, halve the shallot, and slice the lemongrass into 5cm pieces. Add to the water.
Carefully slide the blood cake into the water, then increase the heat to high and bring to a rolling boil for 5 minutes.
Reduce the heat, cover and simmer for 30 minutes.
Uncover and remove the blood cake with a slotted spoon and set aside on a wire rack to drain until cool enough to handle.
Bring a large saucepan of salted water to the boil over high heat.
Cook the noodles according to the packet instructions (they usually take 20–25 minutes). Once cooked, drain them well and rinse under cold water to prevent overcooking.

Slice the meat from the beef ribs into thin slices against the grain, discarding any large fatty bits. Remove the skin from the pork knuckle and shred the pork meat. Slice the skin into thin slices also.
Slice the blood cake thinly and then into smaller cubes.
If using banana flower, remove the outer tough leaves and discard, then peel off a few of the tender leaves. Pile them on top of each other and chiffonade them finely.

To serve, briefly blanch some noodles in boiling water to reheat them. Place the noodles in a large bowl, top with slices of the meat and blood cake, then ladle over the hot, spicy broth. Garnish with coriander, Vietnamese mint, bean sprouts, banana flower and a wedge of lime.
Air Fryers Are More Useful Than You Think
black vinegar and soy dipping sauce, to serve
Place enough water in a wide saucepan to submerge pork and place over medium-high heat.
Bring to a boil, then add the pork, skin side down, and cook for 1 minute, until the skin changes colour.
Carefully turn pork over and cook for a further 30 seconds. Transfer the pork to a large bowl of iced water, and use a sharp knife to scrape off any residue on the skin surface.
Remove from the bowl and place onto paper towels. Pat the pork dry with a paper towel.
Turn pork over and score the meat with 5mm (0.2in) deep slits at 2.5cm (1 in) wide crossways and vertically to make squares. Take care not to cut through the skin.

Do not be concerned if some liquid remains visible immediately after baking.

The dish can be served the same day after resting, but it will be softer and more difficult to portion cleanly.
Allow the potatoes to cool completely.
Reheat for approximately 45 minutes, or until the center reaches: 150°F / 65°C
Watch the surface while reheating. If it begins becoming too brown, place another parchment-paper cartouche directly over the top.
Brush the warm potatoes lightly with clarified butter.
Cut into wedges or generous portions.
Sausage Patties So Delicious, the Eggs Are Just a Side Dish!
3 lbs boneless pork shoulder 1.36 kilograms (trimmed of sinew and cut into grinder-size pieces)
9½ oz pork belly fat 272 grams (cut into grinder-size pieces (added pork-belly fat at approximately 20% of the pork shoulder weight))
1½ tbsp kosher salt — 24 grams ( 1.5% of the combined meat-and-fat weight)
2 tbsp packed dark brown sugar —25 grams
Toast the fennel seeds, coriander seeds, anise seeds, and black peppercorns in a dry skillet over medium-low heat for about 1 minute, just until they become fragrant.Do not allow them to burn.
Transfer the spices to a spice grinder and grind until very fine.

Combine the pork shoulder and pork-belly fat with: - Ground toasted spices - Kosher salt - Red pepper flakes - Sweet Hungarian paprika - Dark brown sugar - Basil - Oregano - Fresh garlicMix thoroughly until the meat and fat are evenly coated with the seasonings.

Cover and refrigerate for at least 8 to 10 hours, preferably overnight.This resting period allows the flavors to penetrate the meatand allows the salt to begin extracting the proteins that help the sausage bind together naturally.
Shortly before grinding, place the seasoned meat and fat in the freezer until they are extremely cold and slightly frozen around the edges, but not frozen solid.
Separate the lean pork and fat enough that you can alternate them as you grind.
Note: Chef Jean-Pierre uses approximately a 3/16-inch grinder plate. A ¼-inch plate can also be used if you prefer a coarser sausage.

Feed approximately:3 to 4 pieces lean pork → 1 piece pork belly fatContinue alternating until everything has been ground.Feed the meat gently into the grinder rather than forcing it through. Keep the receiving bowl nested over ice.
Knead to Develop the Natural Bind:
Knead the ground sausage mixture by hand for approximately 1to 2 minutes.

Fold the mixture toward the center just as you would knead bread dough.Stop when the sausage: - Becomes noticeably tacky - Begins sticking to your hand - Begins sticking to the sides of the bowlThis develops the natural protein bind so you do not need added water or commercial binders.
Return the sausage mixture to: - Refrigerator: approximately 20 minutes or - Freezer: approximately 30–45 minutesThe sausage should become very cold and firm enough to portion cleanly.

Using a cold No. 12 or No. 14 scoop, portion approximately:2½ ounces / 70 grams per pattyPack the sausage firmly into the scoop before releasing it onto a parchment-lined sheet pan.This packing step matters because Chef says loosely packed portions will not form as cleanly into patties.
Place the portioned sausage back into the freezer until the portions become firm but not completely frozen solid.This makes them much easier to shape without sticking or falling apart.

Place each portion inside a round cookie cutter.Flatten it evenly using: - A cold meat pounder - A patty press - Or your handIf the sausage begins sticking, lightly moisten the tools with ice water.Remove the cutter to reveal an evenly shaped patty.

Arrange the finished patties in a single layer and freeze until firm.Once firm, transfer them to: - Resealable freezer bags - Vacuum-sealed bags - Reusable vacuum-storage bagsRemove as much air as possible before returning them to the freezer.
Prepare the Frozen Patties for Cooking:
Thaw the patties for approximately 30 minutes in the refrigerator, leaving them cold and still partially frozen. Handle them gently while soft.
Place the patties in a skillet over low to medium-lowheat. - Cook them slowly until: - Beautifully browned on the first side - Browned on the second side - Cooked through
These Stuffed Tomatoes Are as Delicious as They Are Gorgeous! 😉
1 lb spicy Italian chicken sausage (454g) (or sausage of choice)
1 orange bell pepper (cut into small dice )
½ cup finely grated Pecorino Romano or Parmigiano-Reggiano (50g)
Chicken stock (only as needed to moisten the filling )
Salt and freshly ground black pepper (to taste)
2 cups chicken stock (480ml) (plus more only if needed )
Add the chicken stock and butter to a saucepan and bring to a boil.
Reduce to a gentle simmer, add the barley, cover, and cook until the Barley is tender and the Stock has been absorbed, approximately 10 to 12 minutes.
Remove from the heat and let it stand for another 5 minutes. The barley must still be firm to the bite. Not undercooked, but just like you cook pasta Al dente.
Cut a thin, level slice from the top of each tomato. Save the tops for the final presentation.
Using a paring knife, melon baller, or spoon, carefully remove the seeds, pulp, and as much of the white membrane as possible without piercing the walls.
Turn the hollowed tomatoes upside down and allow them to drain for 10–15minutes.

If you accidentally pierce the bottom of a Tomato while hollowing it, fold a small piece of aluminum foil into a little patch or shallow cup and place it underneath the Tomato, directly beneath the hole. Gently mold the foil around the bottom so it supports the Tomato and helps keep the filling from leaking into the baking dish.
Place the drained tomatoes upright in the baking dish.
Rub a small amount of olive oil inside and outside each tomato.
Season the inside of each tomato with salt and pepper.
Remember, my friends, the Tomatoes do not come seasoned!
Preheat the oven to 400°F (205°C). Lightly oil a baking dish.½
Heat the Olive Oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the Sausage, break it into small pieces, and cook until beautifully golden brown.
Add the Onion and continue cooking until it begins to caramelize. This could easily take 15 to 20 minutes.
Add the Orange Bell Pepper and Spinach and cook until the Pepper is tender and the Spinach has wilted.
Add the Garlic and Thyme near the end so the Garlic keeps its beautiful fragrance.
Stir in the Basil, remove the pan from the heat, and let the mixture cool slightly.
Combine the cooked Barley, Sausage mixture, Breadcrumbs, and most of the grated Cheese in a large bowl. Mix thoroughly.
The filling should be moist but not wet. Add only a small splash of Chicken Stock if it seems dry. Taste and adjust the seasoning.
Now add the lightly beaten egg and mix until evenly incorporated
Check the consistency. The filling should be moist but not wet. Add only a small splash of Chicken Stock if it seems dry.
Pack the filling firmly into the Tomatoes and mound it slightly above the rims. Sprinkle with the remaining Cheese.
Bake without the Tomato tops for approximately 1 hour.
Brush the reserved tops with Olive Oil, place them on the Tomatoes, and bake for another 15 minutes, or until the Tomatoes are tender and the filling reaches at least 150°F (66°C).
Handle the Tomatoes carefully because they become delicate as they cook. Serve immediately.
How to make the Yellow Pepper Coulis:
Heat the Olive Oil in a saucepan over medium-low heat.
Add the Onion and sweat it until soft and translucent, but do not caramelize it. We want a beautiful yellow sauce, my friends—not a brown one!
Add the Shallot and Yellow Bell Peppers, season lightly with Salt and Pepper, and cook for a few minutes.
Add the Garlic only when the liquid is ready, then immediately pour in the Chicken Stock.
Simmer gently until the Peppers are completely tender, adding a little more Stock only if necessary.
Transfer the mixture to a blender and purée until very smooth. Add a small amount of Chicken Stock only if the Coulis is too thick.
OPTIONAL: For an elegant restaurant-quality texture, press the Coulis through a fine-mesh strainer or chinois.
Whisk in the Butter. Do not boil it after adding the Butter.
Spoon the Yellow Pepper Coulis onto each plate and place a Stuffed Tomato in the center.
Add the Tomato top for presentation and serve immediately.
Champagne Chicken Worth Licking the Plate For!
2 tbsp clarified butter or cooking oil (30ml)
Salt and freshly ground black pepper (to taste)
1 cup Champagne or dry sparkling wine (240ml)
1 to 2 tbsp cooked roux (15 to 30g) (as needed)
Mashed potatoes, rice, or sautéed spinach

Season the Chicken Breasts directly with Salt and Pepper. Dredge them lightly in the Flour and shake off any excess.Seasoning the Chicken instead of the Flour gives you better control and ensures the seasoning stays where you need it.

Heat the clarified butter or oil in an ovenproof frying pan to approximately 365°F/ 185°C.Place the Chicken Breasts in the pan with the smooth, attractive presentation side facing down. Sear until beautifully golden, then turn them over and sear the second side.

Transfer the pan to the oven and roast until the Chicken reaches an internal temperature of approximately 155–160°F / 68–71°C.Depending on the thickness of the Chicken Breasts, this may take approximately 15 to 20 minutes.Transfer the Chicken to a plate and allow it to rest. Carryover cooking will continue raising the internal temperature toward 165°F/ 74°C without unnecessarily drying out the meat.

While the Chicken is cooking, prepare the sauce.Melt the butter in a separate frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the Mushrooms, season lightly with Salt and Pepper, and sauté until they release their water.Continue cooking until most of that moisture has evaporated.Do not add the Shallots at the beginning. Mushrooms contain a great deal of water, and the delicate Shallots could overcook or burn before that moisture evaporates.
Add the Shallot and cook gently until softened and fragrant.
Add the Garlic and cook only until it releases its fragrance.Stir in the fresh Tarragon.

Add the Champagne and bring it to a boil.Allow it to reduce substantially—at least by half and, if necessary, even further—until it smells and tastes pleasant rather than raw.Whether you use Champagne or regular White Wine, proper reduction is essential before adding the remaining liquids.
Add the Stock, Cream, and Thickener:
Add the Chicken Stock followed by the Heavy Cream.Bring the sauce to a gentle boil and allow it to reduce slightly.

Whisk in enough Cooked Roux to give the sauce a consistency that coats the utensil rather than running like water.If you do not have Cooked Roux, you can use: * Cornstarch * Arrowroot * Tapioca Starch * Potato Starch Add the thickener gradually so you can control the final consistency.
Finish the Champagne Mustard Cream Sauce:

Reduce the heat and stir in the Dijon Mustard and Parmigiano-Reggiano.The Dijon is primarily there for flavor and binding; it is not the main thickener, so there is no reason to cook it for a long time.Allow the cheese to melt into the sauce.Taste and adjust the Mustard, Salt, Pepper, Cream, and Cheese as necessary. The Mustard should be noticeably present, but the sauce should remain balanced.

Once the sauce tastes right and has the proper consistency, turn off the heat.Whisk in the finishing Butter until the sauce is smooth, glossy, and creamy.Do not boil the sauce after adding the finishing butter, or it will separate.
Allow the Chicken to rest before slicing.This gives carryover cooking time to finish the Chicken and helps preserve its juices.Slice the rested Chicken Breasts just before plating.

Spoon the Champagne Mustard Sauce onto the plate, alongside the Chicken, or over the Chicken according to your preference.Serve with Duchess Potatoes and maple-glazed Carrots, or accompany the Chicken with Mashed Potatoes, sautéed Spinach, or your preferred vegetables and starch.
Buttery, Creamy Duchess Potatoes Baked to Golden Perfection!
3 lb Yukon Gold Potatoes (,peeled and cut into large, evenly sized pieces - 1.36kg)
¼ tsp Ground White Pepper (or to taste - 0.5g)
½ cup Hot Milk (only if absolutely necessary - 120ml)

Place the Potatoes in a large pot and cover them with cold water. Starting them in cold water allows the Potatoes to cook evenly from the outside to the center.Bring the water to a boil, reduce the heat, and cook gently until the Potatoes are completely tender. A knife should pass through them without resistance.

Drain the Potatoes very well. Return them briefly to the warm pot so the remaining moisture can evaporate.Excess water will make the mashed Potatoes loose and prevent the Pommes Duchesse from holding their shape.

Rice the Potatoes - While the Potatoes are still warm, pass them through a potato ricer or food mill. This is how we create that beautiful, smooth texture.Do not use a food processor, my friends, unless you are planning to hang wallpaper!

Add the Butter and Seasonings - Add the softened Butter, Salt and White Pepper. Mix gently until the Butter has incorporated and the Potatoes are smooth.Only add the Hot Milk if the Potatoes are unusually dry and need it. For Pommes Duchesse, use as little Milk as possible because a softer mashed potato mixture will not hold its piped shape.
Cool the Potatoes Slightly - Allow the mashed Potatoes to cool slightly before adding the remaining ingredients.They should be warm but not hot enough to cook the EggYolks.

Add the Egg Yolks and Nutmeg - Add the freshly grated Nutmeg and Egg Yolks. Mix thoroughly until the mixture is smooth and evenly combined.Taste and adjust the Salt and White Pepper before filling the pastry bag.

Prepare and Fill the Pastry Bag - Twist the pastry bag immediately above the piping tip before filling it. Spoon in the Potato mixture, untwist the bag, and squeeze out any trapped air.Air pockets will interrupt the piping and leave bubbles in the finished Potatoes.
Pipe and Chill the Pommes Duchesse:

Pipe the Potatoes - Pipe the mixture onto the prepared baking sheet, leaving some room between each portion because they will expand slightly.Pipe individual rosettes, tall spirals, or rings that can later be filled with gravy.
Chill Until Firm - Refrigerate the piped Potatoes for approximately 20 to 30 minutes, or until they become firm and hold their shape.
Preheat the Oven - While the Pommes Duchesse are chilling, preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C).

Bake Until Golden - Bake the chilled Pommes Duchesse at 425°F (220°C) for approximately 20 to 25 minutes, or until the ridges are lightly golden brown.Bake them a little longer if you prefer a darker crust. The goal is a lightly crisp exterior while the inside remains smooth and creamy.
Cool and Refrigerate - If preparing them in advance, allow the baked Pommes Duchesse to cool completely so the steam can escape.Cover and refrigerate until needed.

Butter, Reheat and Serve - Shortly before serving, gently brush the firm Potatoes with the Melted Butter.Return them to a 375°F (190°C) oven until heated through and beautifully glossy.Garnish with Parsley or Parmesan Cheese, if desired.
Carrots Good Enough to Serve for Dessert!
2 lb fresh carrots (preferablywith the tops attached, peeled — 900 g)
6-8 sprigs fresh thyme (plus additional thyme for garnish)
1 tsp koshe rsalt (or to taste — 5 g)
4 cup Chicken stock, vegetable stock, or water (enough to barely cover the carrots 950ml)

Trim the carrot tops, leaving approximately ½ inch attached for presentation. Peel the carrots and carefully clean around the remaining green stems. If you like, use a paring knife to shape and smooth the ends. This is certainly not necessary, but it makes them look elegant.
Arrange the carrots in a wide, shallow pan in a single layer. Add the thinly sliced garlic, peppercorns, fresh thyme, butter, salt, maple syrup, and nutmeg.

Pour in just enough chicken stock to barely cover the carrots. Vegetable stock or water will also work, but the chicken stock gives us another opportunity to add flavor—and you know how I feel about missed opportunities!

Cover the carrots with a parchment-paper cartouche or a tight-fitting lid. To make a cartouche, fold a square of parchment paper into a narrow triangle, measure it from the center to the edge of your pan, and trim it into a circle. Cut a small hole in the center to allow a little steam to escape.

Bring the liquid to a very gentle simmer over low heat. Cook until the carrots are tender when pierced with a thin knife, approximately 25 to 40 minutes depending on their size and freshness. I like mine very tender, but cook them to the texture that makes you happy.
Carefully transfer the carrots to a serving platter. Spoon a little of the flavorful cooking broth over them and finish with additional butter, if desired.
Garnish with a few fresh thyme leaves. Do not add too much, or your guests will think you are serving thyme with carrots!
6 Salad Dressings So Good, You Could Drink Them!
¾ Cup Sour Cream (or ¾ Cup (180ml) Crème Fraîche)
¼ Cup Cultured Buttermilk (plus more as needed)
1 ½ tbsp Fresh Lemon Juice (or more to taste)
½ tsp Kosher Salt (or more to taste)
¼ tsp Freshly Ground Black Pepper (or more to taste)
In a mixing bowl, combine the mayonnaise and sour cream until smooth.
Add the cultured buttermilk and mix thoroughly. The dressing should be creamy and pourable, but not thin. Add a little more buttermilk if you prefer a looser consistency.
Add the red onion, garlic, dill, chives, parsley, lemon juice, salt, and black pepper. Mix until everything is evenly distributed.
Taste the dressing. Add more lemon juice if it needs brightness and adjust the salt and pepper as necessary. The acidity wakes up the herbs and prevents the dressing from tasting heavy.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours before serving. The garlic, onion, and herbs need time to release their flavors into the dressing.
The Secret to Juicy Pork Milanese Every Time
24 oz 4 boneless pork loin chops (approximately 6 ounces / 170 grams each)
4 cups cold water (960 milliliters or enoughto submerge the pork)
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper (to taste)
1/4 cup garlic-infusedolive oil or neutral frying oil (60 milliliters plus more as needed)
1 tbsp Sicilian lemon balsamic vinegar, white balsamic vinegar, white wine vinegar, or red wine vinegar
1/4 cup garlic-infused olive oil or extra-virgin olive oil (60 milliliters )
In a glass or other nonreactive container, combine the cold water, kosher salt, brown sugar, and smashed garlic. Stir until the salt and sugar have dissolved.
Trim the exterior fat from the pork chops, if desired.
Place each pork chop between two sheets of plastic wrap. Pound it gently and evenly until it is approximately ¼ inch / 6 millimeters thick.
Place the pork cutlets in the brine, making sure they are completely submerged. Cover and refrigerate for 2 to 2½ hours.
Remove the pork from the brine. Dry each cutlet extremely well with paper towels, repeating as necessary until no surface moisture remains.

Preheat the oven to 375°F / 190°C. The oven will only be needed if the pork does not reach the proper internal temperature in the skillet or if the cooked cutlets need to be held briefly before serving.

Place the panko and Parmigiano-Reggiano in a food processor. Pulse briefly until the breadcrumbs are slightly finer and the cheese is evenly incorporated. Transfer the mixture to a shallow dish and season lightly with salt and pepper.
Place the flour in a second shallow dish and the beaten eggs in a third.
Use separate tongs for the flour and egg mixtures to keep the breading station as clean as possible.
Coat each pork cutlet completely in flour and shake off the excess.
Dip the floured pork into the beaten eggs. Check that the entire surface is covered, including any dry spots, and allow the excess egg to drip away.
Place the cutlet in the panko-Parmesan mixture. Spoon breadcrumbs over the top before touching the pork, then press gently to create an even coating.
Pour enough oil into a large skillet to coat the bottom generously. Heat the oil to 365°F / 185°C. Without a thermometer, look for oil that is shimmering and moving slightly.
Working in batches, gently lay each breaded cutlet into the skillet, laying it down away from you to avoid splashing.
Cook until the underside is deeply golden brown, approximately 2–3 minutes.
Carefully turn each cutlet with a wide spatula to avoid disturbing the crust. Cook until the second side is golden brown, approximately 2 minutes.
Transfer the cooked cutlets to a baking sheet lined with parchment paper or a silicone baking mat.
Check the internal temperature. The pork should reach at least 145°F / 63°C. The chef recommends a finished temperature between approximately 145°F and 155°F.
If necessary, place the cutlets in the 375°F / 190°C oven for a few minutes. Remove them as soon as they reach the proper temperature to avoid drying out the pork.
In a small bowl, combine the lemon juice and vinegar.
Stir in the garlic-infused olive oil. Mix the vinaigrette lightly rather than fully emulsifying it. A thick, heavy dressing can weigh down and wilt the arugula.
Just before serving, place the arugula, diced tomatoes, and sliced red onion in a bowl.
Add only enough vinaigrette to coat the vegetables lightly. Season with salt and freshly ground black pepper, then toss gently.
Place one Pork Scallopini Milanese on each plate.
Squeeze fresh lemon juice over the pork or onto the plate beneath it.
Top each cutlet with a small mound of arugula salad and serve immediately while the crust is hot and crisp.
The Shepherd’s Pie That Makes You Look Like You Went to Culinary School! 😉
1 1/2 cups canned chopped tomatoes (crushed by hand)
fresh basil (chopped and divided, to taste)
Pecorino Romano or Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese (freshlygrated, to taste)
Remove the sausage from its casing and break it into small pieces.
Dice the onions, yellow squash, zucchini, eggplant, and bell peppers.
Mince the garlic, halve the cherry tomatoes, and crush the canned chopped tomatoes by hand.
Chop the fresh herbs and basil. Keep the chopped basil covered with a slightly damp paper towel so it does not dry out.
Peel the eggplant in alternating strips, leaving a small amount of skin attached. You may leave all the skin on, but too much can sometimes remain tough.
Prepare the mashed potatoes and keep them warm enough to spread or pipe easily.
Heat a large sauté pan over medium-high heat.
Add the sausage and cook until it begins to brown and releases enough fat to sauté the onions.
Continue cooking until the sausage and onions are nicely caramelized.
When using only one pan, transfer the browned sausage and onions to a bowl before cooking the vegetables. This prevents overcrowding.
Caramelize the Yellow Squash and Zucchini:
Heat a large skillet to approximately 365°F (185°C).
Add enough olive oil to coat the bottom of the pan.
Add the yellow squash and season lightly with salt and freshly ground black pepper.
Sauté until the squash develops a golden-brown exterior.
Add the zucchini and continue sautéing until both vegetables are properly caramelized.
Do not overcrowd the pan or add the tomatoes yet. The vegetables need room for their moisture to evaporate so they brown instead of steam.
Add the red and green bell peppers to the squash and zucchini.
Cook briefly, allowing the peppers to soften while retaining some texture.
Remove the vegetables from the pan when they are properly caramelized.
Heat a little olive oil in a separate skillet.
Sauté until the eggplant is tender and beautifully golden brown.
Eggplant absorbs oil quickly, so add a small additional amount of olive oil when necessary.
Cook each vegetable separately, removing one batch before adding the next. It takes longer, but it allows every vegetable to caramelize correctly.
Place the sausage, onions, yellow squash, zucchini, bell peppers, and eggplant in a large pot.
Cook only until the garlic becomes fragrant.
As soon as you smell the garlic, add the fresh thyme and Herbes de Provence.
Do not let the garlic burn.
Immediately add the cherry tomatoes and chopped tomatoes.
Reduce the heat and stir everything together.
Cook the ratatouille gently for 45 minutes to 1 hour.
Allow the vegetables, sausage, tomatoes, and herbs to slowly cook together until the vegetables are tender and the flavors have married.
Add approximately half of the chopped basil during the simmer.
Reserve the remaining basil for the end. The cooked basil creates a deep, mellow flavor, while the fresh basil provides a brighter aroma.
When the vegetables are tender and the flavors have come together, stir in the remaining fresh basil.
Begin with a small quantity because the heat level varies considerably between brands.
Taste the filling and adjust the salt and freshly ground black pepper as needed.
Lightly butter a lasagna-style baking dish.
Spread or pipe one layer of mashed potatoes across the bottom of the dish.
Sprinkle a light layer of Pecorino Romano or Parmigiano-Reggiano over the potatoes.
Spoon the sausage ratatouille evenly over the mashed potatoes.
Leave enough room at the top for the final potato layer.
Spread or pipe the remaining mashed potatoes over the ratatouille.
Finish with another layer of freshly grated cheese.
Place the assembled shepherd’s pie in the preheated 375°F (190°C) oven.
Bake until the filling is thoroughly heated and the mashed-potato topping is beautifully golden brown.
The shepherd’s pie may be fully assembled in advance and refrigerated until needed.
Before baking a refrigerated casserole, allow it to lose some of its chill.
Reheat it in a 375°F (190°C) oven until the center reaches approximately 155–160°F (68–71°C).
Use an instant-read thermometer rather than relying on a fixed baking time. The exact time depends on the casserole’s size, depth, and starting temperature.
Allow the shepherd’s pie to rest before cutting and serving.
The ratatouille and mashed potatoes will be extremely hot.
Resting also helps the layers settle and makes the portions easier to serve.
Serve warm as a complete meal or accompany it with a simple green salad, roasted vegetables, or crusty French bread.
Massaman Beef Thai Curry With French Love | Chef Jean-Pierre
1¾ lb chuck roast, trimmed and cut into large bite-size pieces
1 large onion, sliced into thin strips
3 tbsp store-bought Massaman curry paste (or homemade)
1½ cup coconut milk, divided (1 cup for stewing, ½ cup for finishing)
2½ cup beef stock (enough to just cover the meat)
1 red chili pepper, finely chopped (optional for heat)
6 thin slices fresh galangal (or substitute ginger if unavailable)
1 small bell pepper, sliced (optional, for color)
1 medium orange sweet potato, peeled and cubed
1 medium white sweet potato, peeled and cubed
½ cup roasted unsalted peanuts, coarsely chopped
Sear the beef in batches, without crowding the pan. Let it sit undisturbed until a dark brown crust forms. This Maillard reaction creates rich, deep flavor. Set the beef aside once browned.
In a Dutch oven, heat olive oil over medium heat.
Add the sliced onions and cook until deeply golden and caramelized. This adds sweetness and depth to the curry base.
Add the Massaman curry paste and sauté for about 1 minute to release its oils and intensify its flavor.
Pour in 1 cup of coconut milk and reduce the heat to low. Stir to combine.
Return the seared beef to the pot.
Add enough beef stock to just cover the meat.
Stir in tamarind concentrate, chopped garlic, chopped chili, brown sugar, and fish sauce.
Add galangal slices and stir well. Optional: stir in bell peppers for extra color.
Bring the mixture to a gentle simmer.
Cook uncovered or partially covered on low heat for about 2 hours, or until the beef is fork-tender.
Check occasionally and add more beef stock or coconut milk as needed to prevent drying out.
Once the beef is nearly done, stir in the chopped peanuts and lime zest.
Add both types of sweet potatoes. Simmer for another 15–20 minutes, or until potatoes are tender.
Remove the galangal slices before serving—they’re flavorful but tough!
Garnish with parsley and extra peanuts if desired.
Flaky, Juicy, Buttery Fish in Minutes, EVERY TIME! | Chef Jean-Pierre
14 oz - 2 skin-on Snapper Fillets (about 6 to 8 ounces each)
Salt (a bit generous, especially on the skin side)
Dry Your Fish Like It Owes You Money:

Dry the fish extremely well. I’m serious, friends—no mercy here. Pat both sides thoroughly with paper towels. If it’s wet, it’ll steam. And steamed skin is floppy. We want golden and crispy, not sad and soggy.
Salt both sides, a bit more on the skin side. Not too much—this isn’t the Dead Sea—but give it enough so the skin crisps up beautifully. It’s all about texture!
Preheat the Pan and Add Clarified Butter:

Get your pan to about 300°F (150°C). Medium to medium-high heat is your friend. Add clarified butter—because if you use regular butter at this point, you’ll burn it before your fish even gets cozy in the pan.
Lay the fish in the pan skin-side down. Press it down with a spatula or a weight for the first few seconds to prevent curling.

Here comes the magic: As soon as that skin sets and starts to get golden (you’ll hear it sizzling), start basting the top of the fish with the hot butter. Tilt the pan, scoop the butter with a spoon, and drizzle it over the fillet. This builds flavor, helps cook the top gently, and keeps everything moist.

At about the 3-minute mark, start checking the internal temperature. Insert a thermometer into the thickest part of the fish. Chef’s rule: remove it at 114°F (46°C)—never let it go above 120°F (49°C). It will rise a few more degrees while resting. If you guess, you’re gambling with greatness!
Once the skin is golden and crispy and the temp is nearing 114°F, gently flip the fish. Let it kiss the pan briefly on the flesh side—just enough to finish cooking and get warm all the way through.
Tilt the pan and baste the top with the hot butter. Lower the heat slightly.

While the fish finishes cooking, zest your lemon and segment it. Be sure to remove all the white pith—it’s bitter and doesn’t belong in our happy little sauce. Save those segments for the final touch.
Remove the Fish and Build the Sauce:
Use a thermometer and DO NOT go above 120°F (49°C) in the center. Take the fish out around 114°F—it will continue to cook slightly after removing from the heat.

Once you remove the fish, pour out the clarified butter. Return the pan to medium-low heat. Add whole unsalted butter and let it melt gently. Then stir in: > Capers > Optional caper brine > Lemon juice > Lemon zest > Lemon segments > A pinch of salt > Cracked black pepper > Fresh parsleyLet the flavors marry and warm up. You’ll see the sauce turn silky and bright. Oh yes, my friends.

Serve the fish skin side up (show off that crisp!) or down if you’re feeling modest. Spoon the warm sauce generously over and around the fillet. Don’t be shy—it’s called lemon caper butter for a reason!
Chicken Marengo: A Classic French Dish, Napoleon’s Favorite Chicken? | Chef Jean-Pierre
1 tbsp chopped garlic (or 2 or 3 teaspoons, who's counting?)
5 lb chicken (1 whole chicken cut into 6–8 pieces, skin removed if preferred)
salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
2 cups dry white wine (don’t drink it all—save some for the pan!) (wine you enjoy drinking only - NO cooking wines!)
18 - 20 oz peeled and chopped San Marzano tomatoes
1 cup chicken stock (start with one, add more if needed)
In a large skillet over medium-high heat, sauté the diced onion in a little olive oil until translucent and slightly golden.
Add the sliced mushrooms and season with salt and pepper. Cook until they release most of their moisture and begin to brown.
While the vegetables are cooking, dredge the chicken pieces in seasoned flour.
In a separate skillet, sear the chicken over medium-high heat until golden brown on both sides. (No skin if you're braising!)
Once browned, remove the chicken and set it aside.
Return to the vegetable skillet. Add the garlic and cook just until fragrant.
Stir in the thyme and deglaze with the white wine.
Let the wine reduce completely—it should lose its sharp acidity. Taste test with a spoon; if it still bites, keep reducing.
Once the wine is fully reduced, stir in the chopped San Marzano tomatoes, chicken stock, and the bay leaf.
Important: Do not add these before the wine has reduced—you’ll lose that beautiful concentrated flavor.
Nestle the browned chicken pieces into the sauce. Don’t stress about the arrangement—this isn’t a magazine shoot!
Cover the skillet with a lid, reduce heat to very low, and simmer gently until the internal temp hits 165°F—about 35–40 minutes.

4 dozen littleneck clams (fresh, about 2-3inches, Florida’s Cedar Key clams if you can snag ‘em!)
3 cloves garlic (smashed - don’t burn it, friends, I’m watching!)
1 handful parsley stems (save the leaves for later)
3 cups White Wine (no cheap swill, treat the clams right!)
pinch chili flakes (just a whisper, nota shout)
Step1: Prep Those Clams Like a Pro:

Alright, friends, let’s start with the stars of the show—the clams! We’ve got four dozen littleneck clams here, fresh as can be. First, give ‘em a little spa day: soak them in salted water (a nice Mediterranean sea salt works wonders) for two hours—no more, or they’ll get cranky.
My grandma used to toss in some cornmeal, swearing it made them spit out sand, but I’ve tried it both ways and honestly? I don’t notice a difference. Your call!

While they’re soaking, check for duds—any cracked ones go straight to the trash. If one’s open, give it a tickle and a squeeze. If it doesn’t snap shut, it’s a goner. Dead clams? No thanks, We're not running a clam cemetery here!
Step 2: Cook the Clams and Make Liquid Gold:

Now, let’s cook these beauties and whip up that clam juice. Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a big pot over medium heat, toss in 3 smashed garlic cloves—don’t let ‘em burn, or you'll regret it!—and a big handful of parsley stems for flavor.
Then, in go the clams. Pour in a good white wine (think of it as their last happy hour), sprinkle some chili flakes, and crank the heat to bring it to a boil.

Once it’s bubbling, reduce it a bit to kiss some of that alcohol goodbye, then slam a lid on it to steam ‘em. As soon as those clams pop open—bam!—yank ‘em out with tongs. Overcooking? Not on your watch!
Keep some pretty shells for decoration (gotta look good, right?) and set the clams aside. Any that don’t open after a fair chance get tossed—sorry, pals, you had your shot.
Step 3: Strain That Juice Like It’s a Treasure Hunt:

Here’s the magic part, friends—this clam juice is liquid gold! Grab a fine mesh strainer (a chinois if you’re fancy, cheesecloth if you’re desperate) and pour the pot’s contents through it into a bowl.
Sand’s the enemy here, so rub a ladle along the bottom to check for grit. If you spot any, strain it again. No sand in the pasta, thank you very much!
Split this juice into two equal parts—half for the Italian, half for the French. Trust me, this beats that jarred nonsense by a mile.

Tie and prepare the Chicken like Chef did in the video.

6 slices Prosciutto (The Chef used Prosciutto di San Daniele)

Toast baguette slices under a broiler until light golden.

Feast of the Seven Fishes Stew | Chef Jean-Pierre
1 pound Shrimp (U-15 size), peeled and deveined

2 tablespoons Fresh Basil, chopped (plus extra for garnish)

Garlic Crostini (optional): Sliced Baguette brushed with Garlic Butter and toasted
In a large pot, heat the olive oil over medium heat. Sauté the shallots and garlic until fragrant.
Add the white wine and reduce slightly, then stir in the chopped tomatoes, cherry tomatoes, and half the chopped basil.
Season with salt and pepper. Bring the mixture to a boil, then lower the heat to a simmer.
Once the broth is gently simmering, add the grouper, Mahi-Mahi, salmon, and scallops, cooking for 5 minutes. Add the shrimp and continue simmering until they turn opaque.
Stir in the cooked pasta, ensuring it is evenly combined.
At the same time, in a separate covered pot, heat olive oil over medium heat. Sauté the shallots for a couple of minutes, then add the garlic and cook until fragrant.
Pour in the white wine and bring it to a simmer. Add the clams and thyme, covering the pot.

Chocolate Roulade (Bûche de Noël) | Chef Jean-Pierre
½ cup Granulated Sugar, divided in two (the chef did not give you the corrected conversion in grams)

Start by whipping the egg whites and cream of tartar at room temperature until soft peaks form. Gradually add half of the sugar while continuing to whip until stiff but not dry and reserve.

Separately, beat the yolks for a few minutes with the remaining sugar until pale and creamy. Stir in vanilla extract. Fold the reserved egg white and when incorporated sift the cake flour, baking powder, and salt, over the yolk mixture.

To prevent sticking, ensure your cookie sheet is lined with parchment paper and that the paper is coated with non-stick spray or butter and flour. Spread the mixture onto the prepared baking sheet and bake at for 15 minutes or until springy to the touch. Cool slightly before rolling it gently in the parchment to maintain its shape.

Beat softened butter until pale and fluffy. Gradually incorporate cocoa powder, powdered sugar, condensed milk, melted chocolate, and salt. Mix until smooth and creamy and reserve at room temperature until ready to use.

Unroll the cooled cake (keep the paper underneath) and brush lightly with simple syrup if desired. Spread an even layer of buttercream over the surface, then roll tightly using the paper as a guide. Refrigerate the roll for at least 2 hours.

Add Rum and let it cool to room temperature before using. Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 month.

Pour warm cream over the chopped chocolate. Stir until smooth, adjusting the cream quantity for a spreadable consistency. Fold in chopped nuts. Pour the ganache over the chilled roll, spreading evenly. Refrigerate until set.

1 tablespoons Cornstarch mixed with 2 tablespoons (30ml) Water

Prepare the duck by trimming excess skin, removing giblets, and patting it dry. Poke small holes in the skin to help render fat during cooking. Dry-brine the duck by generously salting the skin and inside cavity, then place it uncovered in the refrigerator for 24 hours.

While the duck brines, prepare the duck stock. In a large pot, combine chopped duck neck, wings, onion, carrots, celery, leek, star anise, garlic, and peppercorns. Add water to cover, bring to a boil, reduce the heat and simmer for 3-4 hours. Strain the stock and set reserve.

Rinse the duck in ice water to remove excess salt, pat it dry, and score the skin without cutting into the meat. Place it in a roasting pan or a drying rack on a bed of onion. Roast for 2 hours or until the internal temperature reaches 155°F (68°C).

While the duck roasts, make the glaze. Combine honey, soy sauce, and star anise in a small saucepan and simmer until slightly thickened. Brush the glaze over the duck during the last 10 minutes of roasting and increase the oven temperature to 500°F (260°C) to achieve a golden brown finish.

For the Orange Sauce, combine sugar and vinegar in a saucepan over medium heat to create a caramel. Carefully add the duck stock, orange juices, and orange zest. Simmer until reduced, then thicken with cornstarch slurry. Stir in butter off heat until smooth and glossy.

1 tablespoon White Balsamic Vinegar, White Wine Vinegar or Lemon Juice

Add the butter, salt, pepper, hot sauce (if using), maple syrup, vanilla extract, and nutmeg. Blend until smooth and creamy.
Taste and adjust the balance with white balsamic vinegar or lemon juice to achieve the perfect sweet and tangy harmony.
Serve immediately, shaping as desired on a plate.

Beat the softened cream cheese until smooth. Gradually mix in the pumpkin, sour cream, brown sugars, condensed milk, melted butter, and spices. Add eggs one at a time, ensuring each is fully incorporated. Mix in the Amaretto if desired.
Pour the filling into the cold mold with the prepared crust.
Place the pan in a roasting tray and create a water bath by adding hot water halfway up the sides of the pan.
Bake for 1 hour and 45 minutes. Remove from the oven and allow to cool in the water bath for 3-4 hours at room temperature, then refrigerate for at least 24 hours.

Slice with a hot, clean knife for neat servings.

Place the carrots in a pot of cold water, add a tablespoon of salt, and bring to a boil. Once boiling, reduce the heat and simmer until the carrots are about 90% cooked, just slightly firm to the bite. Drain the carrots well and set aside.

In a skillet, melt the butter, and stir in the orange juice concentrate, honey, balsamic vinegar and the orange zest. Cheesy Green Bean Casserole | Chef Jean-Pierre
1 pound Green Beans, trimmed and cut into halves or thirds

In the same skillet, add the mushrooms, salt and pepper and sauté them until they release their moisture and become light golden brown. Add the ham and cook for a couple minutes.

In another saucepan, melt the butter and whisk in the flour to create a roux and cook it for a couple minutes. Gradually add the milk while whisking continuously for another couple minutes. Add the Brie and the Cheddar, nutmeg and cook at very low heat until smooth and thickened.
Add the cooked bacon, ham, mushrooms and adjust salt and pepper as needed.
Combine the green beans ensuring they are well coated.
Transfer the mixture to a greased 2-quart (2L) baking dish, top with parmesan and bacon bits if desired, and bake for 20 - 25 minutes, or until bubbling and heated through.
Creamy Cheesy Mashed Potato au Gratin | Chef Jean-Pierre
5 pounds Yukon Gold Potatoes, peeled and cut into large chunks

Begin by boiling the Yukon Gold potatoes with garlic cloves in salted water, ensuring the water starts cold to allow even cooking. Cook until fork-tender, then drain well.
Using a potato ricer, process the potatoes and garlic into a large mixing bowl.
While the potatoes are still hot, mix in the Gruyère cheese, butter, salt, and pepper. Adjust seasoning to taste.
Transfer the mashed potato mixture into a greased 2-quart baking dish, smoothing the surface.
Sprinkle the top with Parmesan cheese, panko breadcrumbs, and cooked bacon bits.

1 ounces Parmesan Cheese, grated (plus extra for coating soufflé cups)

5 ½ pounds Acorn Squash, halved and roasted
1 bottle Apple Cider (e.g., Martinelli's Sparkling Cider)

Cut the Acorn Squash in half and remove seeds. Season with salt, pepper, and garlic olive oil.

Deglaze the pot with apple cider. Add the carrots, sweet potatoes, apples, leeks, and celery and the roasted squash.
Cover the vegetables with the stock (just enough to barely cover them)

Risotto in Just 20 Minutes (Orzotto)! | Chef Jean-Pierre
3 cups Mushrooms, sliced (baby portobello and regular)

Bring the vegetable stock to a gentle boil, then add the barley and butter, then reduce to low heat.

Fried Chicken Has Never Been So Good! | Chef Jean-Pierre
2 ½ to 3 lbs Bone-in, skin-on pieces (thighs, drumsticks, breasts, wings) ((about 8 pieces))
¼ cup Fine Cornmeal (optional, for extra crunch)

Friends, don’t go buying those Jurassic Park–sized drumsticks. We want little legs and thighs — 2½–3 pounds total, about 8 pieces. Smaller cooks better, juicier, and you don’t need a chainsaw to eat it.

Into a bowl we go! Finely chopped garlic (no boulders, friends, or they’ll burn), grated fresh ginger, salt, pepper, a whisper of curry, and if you like it naughty — a splash of hot sauce. Pour in 2–3 cups buttermilk. Don’t have buttermilk? Milk plus lemon juice… voilà, magic. Stir it up!
Drop those thighs and legs in the bowl. Coat them well, give them a massage like they’re at a spa.
Now cover and let them rest in the fridge at least 2–4 hours. Overnight if you want to dream about crispy chicken.
Bring Marinated Chicken to Room Temp While Draining in a Colander:

When you’re ready to fry, don’t shock the poor chicken! Take it out of the fridge 30–45 minutes before cooking and drain. Cold chicken into hot oil? That’s like jumping into an icy pool — nobody’s happy.
Place a colander in a bowl and then your marinated chicken in the colander to drain away the excess marinade. (Be sure to hold on to that excess marinade because we are going to use it!)

Now for the crunchy suit! Mix flour, cornstarch, and — if you have it — a little fine cornmeal. Then add garlic powder, ginger powder, paprika, curry, cayenne, Creole seasoning, salt, and pepper. Give it a good whisk. Don’t just dump it on top of the chicken, mix first, my friends, or you’ll have spice islands floating around.
Dip your chicken into the marinade, let it drip into the bowl. And then Into the flour mix it goes — coat it like you’re tucking it into bed. Shake off the excess.

“Oh no, we’re not done, my friends. Back into the buttermilk marinade — then again into the flour mix. Yes, your hands will look like fried chicken mittens. But that double dip gives us the crunch heard ‘round the world.
Heat Oil to 320°F (160°C) in a Deep Pot or Wok:

Get your oil to 320°F. Don’t be impatient! Too hot and you’ll have a chicken that’s bronzed on the outside and raw on the inside. Too cold and it drinks oil like it’s happy hour. Medium-low heat, nice and steady.

Slowly lower 3–4 pieces in. Don’t crowd the jacuzzi, friends, or the oil temp will drop and you’ll have soggy sadness. Cook about 15–20 minutes, flipping halfway. Keep that oil steady, check with your thermometer — 165°F inside for dark meat, even 180°F is fine. Breasts? 155°F is perfect.
Once they hit the perfect internal temperature, out they come, onto a wire rack (not paper towels — we want crisp, not steam bath). Let them rest a few minutes so you don’t incinerate your tongue.
Now, friends… the bite. Listen carefully — CRUNCH! Juicy, crispy, flavorful. Garlic, ginger, curry, all playing in the background like a symphony. Trust me — best fried chicken you’ll ever make.
TRADITIONAL Bolognese From Italy! | Chef Jean-Pierre
Salt and Black Pepper to taste
1 pound Pappardelle or Tagliatelle pasta, cooked according to package directions

Quick & Easy Tuna Casserole | Chef Jean-Pierre

12 oz each Solid White Tuna in Water, drained (2 cans)

Add the rice and sauté it for a few minutes until slightly toasted.

One Pan Lemon Roasted Chicken | Chef Jean-Pierre
2 tablespoons White Balsamic Vinegar ( Chef used Sicilian Lemon White Balsamic)
4 to 6 large Carrots peeled cut into slices about 3/16 “(6mm) thick max

Whisk until well mixed and remove and reserve about ½ for the mixture for the vegetables.
Add the chicken thighs ensuring they are well coated. Marinate in the refrigerator for 2-3 hours max 8 hours.
Prepare the vegetables by cutting the carrots into slices and the potatoes into wedges.

Place the marinated chicken thighs on top of the vegetables.

Form the butter into a log using plastic wrap and refrigerate until firm.

Gnocchi that MELTS in your Mouth! | Chef Jean-Pierre
1/2 to 3/4 cup All-Purpose Flour or 00 Flour (or more if needed (sifted))
Prick a couple holes in each potato to allow moisture to escape and bake for about 1 hour or until fully cooked. Depending in the size it could take 60 to 90 minutes.
Once cooked cut in half to allow to cool slightly, then rice them on your work surface.
Combine about ½ of the flour with the riced potatoes, parmesan cheese, egg yolks, and salt.
Mix gently to avoid developing gluten.
Sprinkle with flour to avoid the dough from being sticky. Form the dough without overworking it to keep the gnocchi light and airy.

Chicken Stuffed with BUTTER (Kiev/kyiv) | Chef Jean-Pierre
Salt and cracked Black Pepper to taste
2 cups Cooking Oil (such as Avocado or Vegetable Oil)

Meanwhile, prepare the chicken breasts by making a pocket in each breast from the side, being careful not to cut through to the other side.
